chapter.name: The Rise of Empires
chapter.blurb: What an empire is, trade and guilds, Magadha and the Nandas, Alexander, the Mauryas, Kautilya, Ashoka and the fragility of empires.

scope_in.item: The rise of Magadha and the Nandas
Life, art and decline of the Mauryas

concepts.name: What is an empire?
concepts.description: The meaning of empire, emperor titles, tributaries and the features and motives of empires.
concepts.idea: An empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms under a powerful ruler who receives tribute.
concepts.rule: The word empire comes from the Latin imperium, meaning supreme power. An empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms or territories ruled by a powerful ruler, often after war. The smaller territories kept their own rulers but paid tribute to the emperor, who ruled from a capital. Sanskrit titles include samraj, adhiraja and rajadhiraja. An empire keeps an army, an administration, makes laws and currency, controls resources and encourages art and learning.
concepts.example: Pataliputra was the capital of a vast empire near modern Patna.

questions.a: Armies, administration and roads are costly, so an emperor needs mines, forests, farms and workers to fund and run the empire.

concepts.name: Trade, trade routes and guilds
concepts.description: Why trade matters to an empire, traded goods, trade routes and shrenis (guilds).
concepts.idea: Trade and guilds funded empires and let merchants organise themselves.
concepts.rule: Armies are costly, so economic activity, especially production and trade, is key to an empire. Trade goods included textiles, spices, agricultural produce, gems, handicrafts and animals, and travelled by land and sea. Traders joined together in guilds (shrenis), associations of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists. A guild had an elected head and executive officers. Guilds made their own rules and the king did not interfere. They brought collaborators instead of competitors.
concepts.example: The Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha were main trade routes.

questions.a: Armies, administration and roads need money, workers and resources, so trade and production supply taxes and strength.

concepts.name: The rise of Magadha and the Nandas
concepts.description: Why Magadha rose, iron and geography, Ajatashatru, Mahapadma Nanda and Dhana Nanda.
concepts.idea: Magadha's resources, iron and rivers made it the base of India's first empire.
concepts.rule: Between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE Magadha in south Bihar rose in importance. Ajatashatru made it a centre of power; the Buddha and Mahavira lived in his time. It had fertile land, forests, elephants, iron ore, and the Ganga and Son rivers for transport. Iron ploughs raised produce and iron weapons strengthened the army. Around the 5th century BCE Mahapadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty and issued coins. The last emperor, Dhana Nanda, was rich but unpopular. Panini composed the Ashtadhyayi around this time.
concepts.example: The Ganga and Son rivers helped transport and trade in Magadha.

concepts.name: Alexander and the Greeks in India
concepts.description: Alexander's campaigns, Porus, the retreat and the meeting with the Gymnosophists.
concepts.idea: Alexander's Indian campaign had limited political impact but opened Indo-Greek contacts.
concepts.rule: Alexander of Macedonia conquered the Persian Empire in 334-331 BCE and his empire spread over three continents. In 327-325 BCE he came to India and defeated Porus in Punjab. When asked how he wished to be treated, Porus said 'Like a King', and Alexander left him as satrap. Fierce resistance and tired soldiers who refused to go on made him retreat; he died in Babylon at 32 in 323 BCE. Satraps were provincial governors. Alexander spared the Gymnosophists after their calm answers.
concepts.example: Alexander's soldiers refused to march towards the Ganga.

concepts.name: Chandragupta Maurya and Kautilya
concepts.description: The rise of the Maurya Empire, Kautilya's story and Megasthenes.
concepts.idea: Chandragupta, advised by Kautilya, overthrew the Nandas and built the Maurya Empire.
concepts.rule: Around 321 BCE, a few years after Alexander left, Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire and took over the Nanda territories. His mentor Kautilya (Chanakya or Vishnugupta) had been a teacher at Taxila and vowed to end the Nanda rule after Dhana Nanda insulted him. Chandragupta made Pataliputra his capital, defeated the Greek satraps in the northwest and built an empire from the northern plains to the Deccan. Megasthenes, a Greek historian and diplomat, wrote Indika.
concepts.example: Megasthenes lived in Chandragupta's court and wrote the book Indika.

concepts.name: Kautilya's Saptanga and ideas of governance
concepts.description: The Arthashastra, the seven parts of a kingdom, welfare of subjects and the countryside.
concepts.idea: Kautilya's Saptanga lists seven parts of a state and puts the people's welfare first.
concepts.rule: The Arthashastra means the science of governance and economics and covers defence, administration, justice, urban planning, agriculture and welfare. The saptanga lists seven parts of a kingdom: the king (swami), ministers and officials (amatya), the territory and population (janapada), fortified towns (durga), the treasury (kosha), the forces (danda) and allies (mitra). He stressed law and order and punishments for corruption. He said the king's happiness lies in the happiness of subjects and that power comes from the countryside.
concepts.example: Kautilya asked the king to reward those who built embankments and bridges in the countryside.

questions.q: 'Power comes from the countryside.' Is this still true? Justify.

concepts.name: Ashoka: the king who chose peace
concepts.description: Ashoka's empire, the Kalinga war, edicts, dhamma and his care for subjects.
concepts.idea: After the Kalinga war Ashoka embraced non-violence and spread dhamma through edicts.
concepts.rule: Ashoka (268-232 BCE), Chandragupta's grandson, expanded the empire to almost the whole subcontinent except the far south. After a ferocious war in Kalinga (modern Odisha) he gave up violence for the path of peace taught by the Buddha and sent emissaries abroad. He issued edicts on rocks and pillars, mostly in Prakrit and the Brahmi script, and called himself Devanampiya Piyadasi. He prohibited cruelty to animals, provided medical care, built rest houses and wells and encouraged tolerance among sects. Dharma means duty, law, truth, order and ethics.
concepts.example: Ashoka planted fruit and shade trees along roads.

questions.q: Explain what dharma meant to Ashoka in simple terms.
questions.a: Dharma means moral law and duties towards family, community and country, and living truthfully in harmony with cosmic order.

questions.q: An officer tortures people without good reason. Ashoka's edict says he should
questions.a: practise impartiality and be fair
o: be promoted to a higher post for being strict
be ignored so that he may do as he likes
be praised by the people for his harsh treatment

questions.q: Explain how Ashoka tried to make sure his officers were fair.
questions.a: He instructed them to be impartial and even-tempered, to gain the affection of men and to avoid imprisoning or torturing without reason, and sent an officer on tour every five years.

questions.q: Why should we not take all of Ashoka's claims literally?
questions.a: Rulers tend to present themselves well in edicts
o: Rulers tend to present themselves well in edicts

questions.q: Compare Ashoka before and after Kalinga.
questions.a: Before, he was ambitious and expanded the empire by war; after seeing the destruction he chose peace and non-violence.

questions.q: Explain how Ashoka's rule matched Kautilya's philosophy.
questions.a: Like Kautilya, Ashoka gave attention to the welfare of subjects through medical care, roads, wells and fair officials, and reached out to them through edicts.

questions.q: Was Ashoka tolerant of other beliefs? Give evidence.
questions.a: Yes, he appointed officers of Dhamma to work among all sects and encouraged sects to accept each other's best teachings.

questions.q: Write an edict in your own words, as Ashoka, about kindness to animals.
questions.a: An edict stating that hunting and cruelty to animals are prohibited and that medical care will be given, signed by Devanampiya Piyadasi.

concepts.name: Life, art and the decline of the Maurya Empire
concepts.description: City and village life in Mauryan times, Mauryan art and symbols, and why empires are fragile.
concepts.idea: The Mauryas built planned cities and great art, but large empires are fragile.
concepts.rule: Cities such as Pataliputra had palaces and planned streets. The Sohagaura copper plate records a granary set up against famine. Megasthenes reports two crops a year, rare famines, wooden houses up to two storeys, signage, couriers and water vessels for fire. The Sarnath lion capital shows four lions, four animals and the dharmachakra and is India's national emblem with the motto satyameva jayate. The Great Stupa at Sanchi shows Mauryan architecture. Empires decline when regions break away, resources are strained or natural calamities strike, and they rest on force.
concepts.example: The dharmachakra of the Sarnath capital appears on India's flag.

questions.q: India's national emblem comes from the Sarnath lion ____.
questions.a: capital

questions.q: The motto of the national emblem is
questions.a: satyameva jayate

questions.q: The Sohagaura copper plate records the setting up of a
questions.a: granary

questions.q: About how long did the Maurya Empire last after Ashoka's death?
questions.a: half a century

questions.q: Why were famines rare in Mauryan times?
questions.a: Two crops a year and well-stocked granaries
o: Two crops a year and well-stocked granaries
No one farmed and so no food was needed
Rain never fell and so people ate less
Food was imported from the other countries

questions.q: Rock and pillar messages of Ashoka were mostly written in ____ script.
questions.a: Brahmi

questions.q: The wheel on the Sarnath capital is the
questions.a: dharmachakra

questions.q: Which is a reason empires decline?
questions.a: Distant regions become independent when demands increase
o: Distant regions become independent when demands increase
Trade grows and the treasury of the empire fills with wealth
Farming increases and the people of the empire are well fed
Roads improve and the rule of the empire becomes easy

questions.q: Describe two features of Mauryan cities.
questions.a: Planned streets with signage, wooden houses up to two storeys, water vessels for fire and couriers for messages.

questions.q: Which structure shows Mauryan architecture?
questions.a: the Great Stupa at Sanchi

questions.q: The four lions on the Sarnath capital symbolise
questions.a: royal power

questions.q: What do the animals and the wheel on the Sarnath capital stand for?
questions.a: The lions symbolise royal power, the four animals are an elephant, bull, horse and lion, and the wheel represents the Buddha's teachings.

questions.q: How did Mauryan farmers stay protected in war?
questions.a: Even if war raged nearby, farmers were protected and agriculture was not disturbed.

questions.q: A stupa's central round structure is called the
questions.a: anda

questions.q: Explain how an economic crisis could break up an empire.
questions.a: A drought or flood cuts revenue and food, so the emperor demands more tribute, resentment grows and distant regions may split away.

questions.q: Why are empires called something of a paradox?
questions.a: They bring unity yet rest on force and are fragile
o: They bring unity yet rest on force and are fragile
They never fight since the rulers keep peace everywhere
They never end once they have been built by a ruler
They are always small and cover only a few villages

questions.q: Give one benefit and one weakness of empires.
questions.a: They can bring political unity and prosperity, but they are usually established by war and maintained by force, making them unstable.

questions.q: Explain the legacy of the Mauryas.
questions.a: They strengthened trade routes and coinage, planned cities, an elaborate administration and promoted art and architecture, including the national emblem.

questions.q: Do you think the Mauryas' achievements outweigh the use of force? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is accepted, weighing unity and prosperity against war and repression.

questions.q: Create a museum label for the Sarnath lion capital.
questions.a: A label with name, place, four lions and four animals, the dharmachakra, and its use as the national emblem.
